about: What we know so far about the first step, from someone getting in touch to their application. Shown at kinderform.org/research. Each source says whether a person has checked the claim against the original, when, and against what. Use null for 'not yet checked'. Edit by pull request; tests/validate_findings.py checks the format. A surviving historical check is bound to the unchanged title, summary and source URL by claim_sha256. This guard does not establish a new human review. Clear checked after editing a claim until a person reviews it again.

findings.title: One hub study found quicker visits, without a clear gain in approvals
findings.summary: In the North East of England, councils recruit foster carers together through a regional hub. The reported share with a first visit within 5 days rose from 29% in 2024 to 50% in 2025. A comparison with similar areas found no statistically significant gain in applications or approvals. This does not show that the true effect is zero. The study assessed a whole hub model; it does not isolate reply speed.

findings.title: Some people drop out when one service hands them on to another
findings.summary: The same evaluation found that the hand-over from the hub to the council was a weak point. Some people who withdrew said communication stopped or dropped off, and it was not clear who should answer their questions. The Department for Education now expects hubs that run the whole journey to give each person a named "journey guide" from enquiry to approval.

findings.title: Applications ask far more than enquiry forms, and most UK application forms are not public
findings.summary: In November 2026 we read 52 application forms and packets in 7 countries. A typical UK application form asked 54 questions, against 8 on a typical UK enquiry form. Every UK application form we read asked about health, but none of the 57 UK enquiry forms did. Most UK application forms are not public: of 41 we found, we could read 6. France's national form asks nothing about health or convictions. A medical certificate goes with it, and the council asks for the criminal record itself.

findings.title: Most fostering applications that finish end in withdrawal, not approval
findings.summary: In England, fostering services received 8,290 applications in the year to 31 March 2025. Of the 5,370 applications that finished that year, services approved 2,050 and 3,290 ended in withdrawal. Applicants withdrew 2,175 of these and services withdrew 1,115. That is 61% of finished applications, not of all applications received. Where the applicant withdrew, 20% said the process was not what they expected.

findings.title: How the first contact feels is what people remember
findings.summary: In research for the Department for Education, people mentioned how their first contact felt more than anything else. Many saw getting in touch as the start of an application, and worried about asking "the wrong question". In an online experiment, every redesigned message did better than typical recruitment wording. But that experiment measured what people said they would do, not what they did.

sources.title: Applying behavioural insights to fostering and adoption in England
sources.by: Kantar Public for the Department for Education

findings.title: Enquiry forms differ a lot in what they ask and what they promise
findings.summary: In November 2026 we read 57 enquiry forms from councils, hubs, independent agencies and adoption agencies across the UK. The shortest asked 3 questions and the longest asked 17. Asking about a spare room depended on the type of service. 8 of the 11 independent agency forms asked about a spare room, but none of the 37 council and hub forms did. Only 7 of the 56 forms where we looked for a reply time said when you would hear back.

findings.title: A named, personal message can change what people do
findings.summary: In a trial at a jobcentre in Bedford, 1,224 jobseekers got a text inviting them to a recruitment event. When the text named their adviser and said a place was booked for them, 26.8% went, against 10.5% for the plainest text. The trial was not about fostering, so the idea needs testing in fostering and adoption before anyone relies on it.

findings.title: Knowing a carer, or simply being asked, starts many people thinking about fostering
findings.summary: A review of research from around the world looked at why people foster. It found that meeting or knowing foster carers is what most often leads people to consider fostering. In an Australian survey of 756 adults, almost 1 in 3 had never considered fostering. They said this was because no one had ever asked them.

findings.title: Some people who go no further say the way the service replied put them off
findings.summary: An Australian study followed up 91 people who had asked about fostering. Only 4% had become carers. The rest split roughly evenly between changes in their own lives and being put off by how the agency responded. The study is old and small, so treat it as a pointer. In the United States, a study of 300 families hoping to adopt from foster care looked at the barriers they met. The families most often reported 3 kinds: the practical steps of the process, how the agency communicated and responded, and emotional support.

findings.title: The relationship with the service shapes whether carers stay
findings.summary: A review of 49 studies looked at why carers keep fostering. It found that the relationship with the agency and support from professionals stand out among the reasons. A Scottish study looked at carers who had stopped fostering. Almost 3 in 5 had stopped because they were unhappy with some part of their fostering service. A 2024 UK survey asked carers if their supervising social worker treated them as an equal. 76% of current carers said yes, against 51% of former carers. This is why we treat the first reply as the start of support, not a separate task.

findings.title: About 1 in 8 approved fostering households in England de-registered in 2025–26, including transfers
findings.summary: In 2025–26, 4,440 of 37,890 mainstream households approved at some point in England de-registered: 12%. Of those 4,440, 3,675 were leavers, 700 transferred and 65 were other. Carers aged 60 or over were 35% of carers who de-registered. Their age alone does not tell us why they left. Among those under 50, 19% left to adopt the child. So de-registration does not always mean a service failed or a household stopped fostering. Early de-registration is one question for a first-step pilot. In 2020–21, 30% of households that de-registered did so within two years of approval.

findings.title: Households in Mockingbird stopped less often, but it has not been tested in a trial
findings.summary: Mockingbird groups foster homes around an experienced carer who offers support and breaks. In an English evaluation of 11 areas from 2016 to 2019, 6% of Mockingbird households stopped (16 of 288). Among similar households, 23% stopped (689 of 2,968). Their odds of stopping were about a fifth as high. It was not a randomised trial, and the households differed: fewer Mockingbird households were newly approved. A later evaluation has published no results that we could find.

findings.title: A review of online surveys found mixed effects from progress bars
findings.summary: A review of 32 experiments with online surveys looked at progress bars. A bar moving at a steady speed did not reliably stop people giving up. A bar that looked slow at first made it worse. In another experiment, fewer people started a survey when told it would take longer. Pages with few questions and designs made for phones lost fewer people. This research is about surveys, not fostering. Someone offering to foster may have stronger reasons to finish.

findings.title: One GP call study links unclear next steps with extra work for callers
findings.summary: A study of 447 recorded calls to three English GP surgeries found two moments when callers had to push for what they needed. One was when no alternative was offered. The other was when the call ended without a summary of what happens next. This happened most at the surgery with the lowest patient satisfaction. It is one study of three surgeries, and it shows a link, not a cause. It is not about fostering. These moments may also arise in fostering calls; that transfer still needs testing.

findings.title: People are most often lost between steps, when contact lapses or nobody reaches them
findings.summary: Our reviews keep finding the same pattern. In the North East of England, some people who withdrew said communication stopped after the hub handed them to the council. At a kidney donor centre in the United States, the largest loss came straight after the first form. The main reason was that the person did not answer the follow-up call. In a study of 157,154 accepted job offers, longer gaps before the start date went with more people never starting. Most of this evidence comes from other fields, or describes what happened without testing a cause. No one has tested it with people who enquire about fostering.

findings.title: Hands-on help improved college enrolment in one US student-aid trial
findings.summary: In a US trial, low-income families were offered help to complete a student aid form. College enrolment among school leavers rose by 8.1 percentage points, from 34.2%. Information alone made no difference. Other application studies found reminder effects of 1 to 3 points. They used different settings and outcomes, so their effect sizes cannot be compared directly. For fostering, the closest step is offering a call to finish an enquiry together. None of these trials is about fostering.

findings.title: Relatives and friends can arrive at a general fostering form, and the UK forms we read do not ask
findings.summary: Most kinship carers do not apply to foster. They step in for a child they know, and the child's social worker usually gets in touch with them. But GOV.UK tells people who want to look after a child in care to ask their council about fostering a child they know. So some relatives and friends reach a general fostering enquiry form. In November 2026 we searched the 48 UK fostering enquiry forms we had read. None asks whether the person already knows the child. Ofsted collects no enquiry figures for kinship households, so nobody knows how many people arrive this way.

findings.title: Most kinship carers say they did not know their legal options when they took on the child
findings.summary: A 2019 survey asked 845 kinship carers about the time they took on the child. Three-quarters said they did not have enough information about their legal options. In a 2022 survey, it was 82%. In a 2025 survey of 1,929 kinship carers, 13% had seen their council's kinship local offer. The legal route affects the support a carer can get. Since June 2026, councils in England must publish a kinship local offer. Statutory guidance says families should get clear information about their legal options at the outset. The surveys come from charities that campaign, and carers chose to take part.

findings.title: For kinship carers, the best-evidenced help is a person who guides them
findings.summary: A navigator is a person who helps a kinship carer find and get support. In November 2026, a federal clearinghouse in the United States rated nine navigator programmes as promising or better. In Washington State, carers in a fuller version of the programme reported better overall wellbeing than carers in the usual service. That study compared two versions of the programme, and carers reported their own wellbeing. England's practice guide for councils recommends specialist support of the same kind. In a 2025 survey, 40% of kinship carers had a named contact at their council. No one has tested a way of handling first contact with kinship carers in England.

findings.title: Our desk search found no trials of follow-up after a real enquiry
findings.summary: Our November 2026 desk search looked for experiments on reply times, contact attempts, follow-up, contact with experienced carers and hand-offs. We found none with real people asking about fostering or adoption. The search was not a systematic review, so it may have missed studies. The closest study we found was a 2022 online test of message wording. It measured what people said they would do. Kinderform hopes to test these ideas openly, with services' agreement. A later desk search also found no study of wording in first fostering calls or replies. It found no published figures on forms started but not sent. These are search results, not proof that none exist.
